replacement.title: Manage the last minute with a lead
replacement.objective: Compare possession options under a stated late-game objective.
replacement.briefing: Navy leads by one with 48 seconds remaining. YOU have controlled possession in a wide neutral-zone lane. The coach asks for a controlled play that preserves defensive support; this does not mean every forward option is forbidden. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing states the lead and remaining time; they are not inferred from the rink.

questions.prompt: What score-and-clock situation is explicitly given?

options.text: Navy trails by two with a full period left
The score is tied and no clock is stated
Navy leads by one with 48 seconds left

questions.explanation: The briefing states the lead and remaining time; they are not inferred from the rink.

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect the stated possession objective?

options.text: The controlled support available through D2 or F3
Gold 1’s pressure toward the carrier
A claim that any attacking pass violates the objective

questions.explanation: The lead changes acceptable risk, but the actual available play still matters.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read for this late-game possession.

options.text: Confirm time, score and available support
Compare pressure on each controlled option
Choose and communicate the next support job

questions.explanation: Confirming the clock, score and support and comparing pressure on each option can overlap as YOU keep scanning; only the final step, choosing and communicating the next support job, has to come after those reads are in. This is not a universal final-minute rule.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare the routes toward D2 and F3.
questions.explanation: The example moves closer to D2 and farther from Gold 1, but farther from F3. Compare the changed routes and the clock before choosing.

questions.prompt: F1 becomes clearly open beyond Gold 1 with room to retain the puck. What changes?

options.text: A controlled forward pass may now fit the objective
The clock makes every forward pass automatically wrong
D2 must receive regardless of the open route

questions.explanation: A lower-risk forward option can be consistent with protecting a lead.

questions.prompt: How would YOU explain a sensible risk tradeoff without reducing it to “never attack with a lead”?
questions.explanation: Use the clock, pressure, support and likely possession outcome; acknowledge more than one viable controlled play.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate with 48 seconds left?

options.text: We value possession, but I will use a clear forward lane
The lead removes every forward option
F1 is the first outlet regardless of the pressure route

questions.explanation: The message balances the stated lead with a conditional forward choice.

questions.prompt: Which two events change the late-game risk?

options.text: Gold pressure closes the support lane
F1 becomes reachable with room
The score stays one goal apart

questions.explanation: Pressure and support change the risk decision while the score remains context.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare forward routes toward F1 and F2.
questions.explanation: The example moves closer to both forwards and closer to Gold 1. Check pressure before treating either route as usable.

questions.prompt: Gold closes F1 but F2 remains open. Explain the late-game branch.
questions.explanation: Name the closed lane, check F2, and choose the lower-risk reachable option while keeping the lead context in mind.

replacement.objective: Assess a late attacking choice without declaring a guaranteed scoring play.
replacement.briefing: Navy trails by one with 32 seconds left and has five skaters on the ice. YOU control at the puck-side point. F1 is near the net, F2 is across the high slot and D2 is the other high player. Navy’s goalie, omitted from this selected-player view, remains in net; no extra attacker is assumed. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing explicitly excludes a goalie pull, avoiding an unstated manpower assumption.

sources.section: Page 1, shot choice, puck management and anticipation
sources.use: Supports age/topic placement only. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

replacement.limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Is an extra attacker part of this stated setup?

options.text: No Navy players are near the net
No, Navy has five skaters and its goalie remains in net
Yes, Navy has six skaters

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly excludes a goalie pull, avoiding an unstated manpower assumption.

questions.prompt: Choose two considerations for generating a remaining chance.

options.text: Whether a shot can reach useful traffic
A certainty that shooting from the point always scores
Whether a pass would create a clearer attempt in time

questions.explanation: Time matters, but a rushed blocked shot and a clearer available connection are different possibilities.

questions.prompt: Arrange a time-aware attacking read.

options.text: Check the remaining clock and immediate lanes
Compare the available shot and connecting pass
Commit to a feasible attempt and support its next touch

questions.explanation: Checking the clock/lanes and comparing the shot against a connecting pass can overlap as YOU scan; only committing to the attempt and supporting its next touch has to come last, once those reads are in. The still setup cannot validate travel times or scoring probability.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a more central point angle.
questions.explanation: The reference changes the shot and pass routes. It may consume time, so it is an illustration rather than a prescribed late-game skate.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 lunges into the shot lane and F2 becomes visible. What should be considered?

options.text: The unchanged shot lane from before the lunge
An automatic hold until the clock expires
A quick checked connection to F2

questions.explanation: The new cue can favour a connection, but the available time and F2’s preparation still matter.

questions.prompt: Why is “get a shot” incomplete feedback in this final-minute scene?
questions.explanation: Explain route, traffic, time and possible next possession; more attempts are not identical chances.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate while trailing late?

options.text: We need a chance; check the lane before forcing it
The deficit makes every shot correct
F2 stays the preferred option even if Gold closes the route

questions.explanation: The call acknowledges the deficit while preserving a scan before risk.

questions.prompt: Which two updates support a remaining chance?

options.text: Gold 1 commits to the carrier
F2 or F3 becomes reachable
The clock alone creates a lane

questions.explanation: Defender commitment and support access create the attacking branch.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a more central point angle toward F2.
questions.explanation: The example is nearer the middle and farther from Gold 1. Check the changed passing route, traffic and remaining time; the point does not establish an open lane.

questions.prompt: Gold blocks F2 but leaves F3 wide. Explain your next read.
questions.explanation: Recheck F3 and the net-side lane, then choose a pass or carry only if it remains reachable; the deficit does not remove that condition.

replacement.title: Attack a power-play entry before the setup forms
replacement.objective: Recognize an available rush option without assuming the unit must first arrange a formation.
replacement.briefing: Navy has five skaters against four. YOU carry a controlled wide entry, F2 offers middle support and F3 trails. The coach permits a rush chance if it is clearly available; the unit is not required to establish an in-zone formation first. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing explicitly permits an early rush option while retaining a lane check.

sources.title: Special Teams Tactics with Mike Guentzel
sources.section: Trouble setting up a power play / scoring from the rush
sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

replacement.limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: What does the stated team instruction permit?

options.text: A clearly available rush chance before a set formation
Only a complete formation before any chance
A guaranteed goal because of five-on-four

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly permits an early rush option while retaining a lane check.

questions.prompt: Which two cues help judge that option?

options.text: A requirement to stop solely because it is a power play
F2’s readiness and route
Gold 1 and Gold 2’s coverage of the entry

questions.explanation: The local read still matters on special teams; the numerical advantage is not an answer key.

questions.prompt: Arrange an entry read under this instruction.

options.text: Read the entry defenders
Compare the immediate chance with retained possession
Attack or settle according to the available picture

questions.explanation: Reading the entry defenders and comparing the immediate chance against retained possession can overlap as YOU carry; only attacking or settling has to come last, once that picture is clear. Both attacking and settling may be reasonable under different cues.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a carrier angle connecting the wide entry to middle support.
questions.explanation: The example changes the relation to F2 and Gold 1. It does not validate a passing window or skating race.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 closes F2 and Gold 1 contains your lane. What could be useful?

options.text: Treat the power play as over
Protect possession and look for the trailing support
Force the old rush pass because the coach permitted a chance

questions.explanation: Permission to attack does not require forcing a chance after its routes close.

questions.prompt: How is “allowed to score from the rush” different from “must shoot immediately”?
questions.explanation: The first preserves choices based on the defenders; the second ignores whether a useful chance actually exists.

questions.prompt: What should YOU say before the permitted rush entry?

options.text: The lane is conditional; F2 and F3 show me the next option
The instruction requires an immediate shot
Gold’s pressure shape stays the same after the entry angle changes

questions.explanation: The call keeps permission separate from a forced action and names support.

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong before using the rush?

options.text: Gold 1 and Gold 2 pressure
F2 or F3 reachability
The power-play label alone

questions.explanation: Pressure and support decide whether the permitted entry is usable.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare the routes toward F2 and trailing F3.
questions.explanation: The example is nearer the middle and closer to F2 and F3, but also closer to Gold 3. Compare pressure and support before choosing a pass.

questions.prompt: Gold closes both visible support lanes. What should YOU reconsider?
questions.explanation: Protect the puck or reset instead of forcing the permitted rush. Permission remains conditional on a reachable lane.

replacement.title: Protect the backdoor during a penalty-kill rotation
replacement.objective: Track a low weak-side threat under a declared penalty-kill responsibility.
replacement.briefing: Navy kills four-on-five. Gold 1 controls at the puck-side half wall, Gold 2 is below the goal line and Gold 3 waits across the low slot. YOU are the weak-side low defender. This drill assigns YOU the weak-side low threat until a teammate confirms an exchange. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 3 is in the weak-side low slot while Gold 1 carries at the puck-side half wall.

Navy kills four-on-five. Gold 1 controls at the puck-side half wall, Gold 2 is below the goal line and Gold 3 waits across the low slot. YOU are the weak-side low defender. This drill assigns YOU the weak-side low threat until a teammate confirms an exchange.

sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

replacement.limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Which attacker is across the low slot from the puck side?

options.text: Gold 1
Gold 4
Gold 3

questions.explanation: Gold 3 is in the weak-side low slot while Gold 1 carries at the puck-side half wall.

questions.prompt: Select two checks before exchanging the low responsibility.

options.text: A teammate’s confirmed coverage
Gold 3’s route near the net
Only the puck below the goal line

questions.explanation: The drill’s handoff condition is explicit; an unconfirmed exchange can leave the weak-side threat unattended.

questions.prompt: Arrange a coverage handoff under this drill plan.

options.text: Identify the moving low threat
Communicate who will cover it
Adjust after coverage is confirmed

questions.explanation: The plan is one teaching constraint, not a claim that every penalty kill uses this handoff.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a net-side weak-side position.
questions.explanation: The example is on the opposite side from Gold 1 and closer to Navy’s net than Gold 3. Recheck Gold 2 and Gold 3 before assuming the low lane is covered.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 receives below the goal line and Gold 3 cuts inward. What needs updating?

options.text: The immediate low pass threat and assigned coverage
The belief that Gold 1 still owns the puck
A requirement for every killer to chase Gold 2

questions.explanation: The new carrier and moving receiver must be read together.

questions.prompt: Name the backdoor or low-slot area YOU are protecting and explain the passing threat.
questions.explanation: Gold 3 is the weak-side low threat in the starting picture. If Gold 2 receives behind the goal line, recheck the route from the new carrier to Gold 3 and communicate any exchange.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call during the low exchange?

options.text: I am tracking Gold 3; confirm who takes the low threat before I switch
The low rotation covers itself
Gold 3 remains the outside reference after the inside cut

questions.explanation: Gold 3 is the assigned weak-side threat; Gold 2 starts behind the goal line. Name the intended handoff and confirm the teammate’s coverage.

questions.prompt: Which two changes require a coverage update?

options.text: Gold 2 moves across the slot
D1 rotates away from the net-side lane
The puck remains below the line

questions.explanation: Attacker movement and teammate rotation change the dangerous lane.

questions.prompt: From the starting picture, compare another net-side position against Gold 3.
questions.explanation: The example remains opposite Gold 1 and closer to Navy’s net than Gold 3. It is slightly nearer Gold 3 than the earlier example; other questions’ hypothetical movements have not occurred in this frame.

questions.prompt: Gold 3 cuts inward as Gold 2 receives below. Explain the handoff.
questions.explanation: Name Gold 3 as the new inside threat, communicate the exchange, and keep the net-side lane covered.

replacement.briefing: F1 has recovered the puck and carries into the neutral zone. YOU are the supporting defender; D2 stays deeper by agreement. F2 is ahead and Gold 3 is recovering near YOU. The drill permits an activation only after secure possession and available support are checked. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing assigns deeper cover to D2 before the activation is considered.

sources.section: PDF page 15, Neutral Zone Regroups: second wave and game situation
sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

replacement.limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Which defender has the explicitly stated deeper-cover role?

options.text: Gold 3
D2
YOU

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns deeper cover to D2 before the activation is considered.

questions.prompt: Choose two checks for joining the attack.

options.text: F1’s quality of possession
The idea that every recovery requires both defenders to go
Whether D2 and recovering pressure support the decision

questions.explanation: Activation is a conditional choice; the source principle does not erase risk.

questions.prompt: Arrange an activation assessment.

options.text: Confirm controlled possession
Check covering support and Gold 3
Join or hold according to the updated picture

questions.explanation: Confirming controlled possession and checking covering support/Gold 3 can overlap as YOU skate; only joining or holding has to come last, once both reads are in. The routine assumes the stated cover plan and still needs realistic timing.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a second-wave supporting lane.
questions.explanation: The example is behind F2 and F3 but slightly ahead of carrier F1, in a different lane. Recheck D2’s cover and Gold 3; arrival timing and a passing window are not established.

questions.prompt: F1 bobbles the puck as Gold 3 accelerates. What deserves a fresh decision?

options.text: The old activation regardless of possession
A belief that D2 can cover every possible turnover alone
Whether to hold or recover instead of continuing up ice

questions.explanation: Possession quality and pressure changed, so the original support choice may no longer fit.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a useful second wave from leaving the play without cover?
questions.explanation: Discuss secure possession, D2’s role, pressure and a reachable support lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before joining the second wave?

options.text: F1 has control and D2 is behind me; call if either changes
The attack makes cover unnecessary
F2 owns the puck

questions.explanation: The message names carrier and cover, the two conditions for activation.

questions.prompt: Which two changes require reassessing the activation?

options.text: F1 loses control
D2 leaves the deeper cover
F2 stays wide

questions.explanation: Possession and cover determine whether the second wave remains responsible.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a second-wave lane behind F1, separate from F3.
questions.explanation: The example stays behind F1 and separate from F3. Check D2’s deeper cover and Gold 3’s recovery before continuing; no open pass is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Gold 3 accelerates as F1 bobbles. What is your new priority?
questions.explanation: Recover or hold the cover first, then re-read F1 and F2. The earlier activation plan is stale.
